trial_name: TTM — Targeted Temperature Management at 33°C versus 36°C after Cardiac Arrest (2013)
citation: Nielsen N, Wetterslev J, Cronberg T, et al. Targeted temperature management at 33°C versus 36°C after cardiac arrest. N Engl J Med. 2013;369:2197-2206.
trial_type: RCT — international, multicenter, parallel-group, open-label, superiority
one_liner: In unconscious adult OHCA survivors, targeting 33°C did not reduce 180-day mortality or improve neurological outcomes compared to targeting 36°C under active fever prevention.

pico.population: Unconscious adult survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause with sustained ROSC >20 minutes.
pico.intervention: Targeted temperature management at 33°C for 28 hours, controlled rewarming to 37°C (0.5°C/hr), and fever prevention through 72 hours post-ROSC.
pico.comparison: Targeted temperature management at 36°C for 28 hours, controlled rewarming to 37°C, and fever prevention through 72 hours post-ROSC.
pico.outcome: Primary: 180-day all-cause mortality. Secondary: 180-day poor neurological outcome (CPC 3–5, mRS 4–6), serious adverse events.

background.existing_knowledge: Mild therapeutic hypothermia (32–34°C) became standard care following 2002 trials showing improved neurological outcomes compared to non-protocolised usual care where fever was common.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty existed whether clinical benefits stemmed from true hypothermia or simply avoidance of hyperthermia, given that deeper cooling causes electrolyte shifts, arrhythmias, coagulopathy, infection, and prolonged sedation.
background.hypothesis: In comatose adult survivors of OHCA of presumed cardiac cause, targeting 33°C improves survival and neurological outcomes compared with targeting 36°C when both groups receive active temperature control.

methods.design: Randomised, international, multicentre (36 ICUs), parallel-group superiority trial with open-label temperature allocation and structured, blinded neuroprognostication.
methods.setting: 36 ICUs across Europe and Australia; enrollment directly from ICU or Emergency Department.

inclusion: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause
exclusion: Time from ROSC to screening >240 minutes

methods.intervention: Active cooling to target 33°C using surface or intravascular devices with sedation/analgesia/anti-shivering. Maintained for 28 hours post-randomisation, rewarmed to 37°C at 0.5°C/hr, with ongoing fever prevention up to 72 hours post-ROSC.
methods.comparison: Active temperature control to maintain 36°C (including warming if needed) using identical timeline: 28-hour maintenance, controlled rewarming to 37°C, and active fever prevention up to 72 hours post-ROSC.
methods.blinding: Treating clinical team was unblinded to target temperature; outcome assessors and neuroprognostication assessors followed a strict protocol designed to minimise bias.
methods.sample_size_power: 900 patients required to detect a hazard ratio of 0.80 for 180-day death (33°C vs 36°C) with 90% power at a two-sided 5% significance level; 950 planned for attrition.
methods.primary_outcome: All-cause mortality through end of trial (180 days).
secondary_outcomes: Poor neurological outcome at 180 days defined by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC 3–5)
Poor neurological outcome at 180 days defined by modified Rankin Scale (mRS 4–6)

headline_bullets: No difference in 180-day all-cause mortality between 33°C and 36°C targets (50% vs 48%; HR 1.06; P=0.51).
Poor neurological outcomes at 180 days were equivalent between groups by CPC (52% vs 53%) and mRS (51% vs 53%).
Hypokalaemia was significantly more frequent in the 33°C group (19% vs 13%; P=0.018).
No prespecified subgroup demonstrated treatment effect modification.

outcomes_table.note: Time-to-event analysis in modified intention-to-treat population
Evaluated among patients with available 180-day CPC
Evaluated among patients with available 180-day mRS

outcomes_table.outcome: Any serious adverse event excluding death (days 1–7)
outcomes_table.note: Collected in supplementary appendix during days 1–7
Electrolyte disturbance related to deeper cooling

safety: Any non-fatal serious adverse event (days 1–7): 93% (33°C) vs 90% (36°C), P=0.086.
Hypokalaemia occurred significantly more frequently in the 33°C group (19% vs 13%; P=0.018).
Early rewarming in the 33°C group occurred for clinical instability: arrhythmia (n=6), severe circulatory instability (n=4), bleeding (n=2), uncontrolled lactate rise (n=2), and urgent CABG (n=1).

domains.notes: Computer-generated assignment with concealed allocation stratified by site; baseline characteristics were well balanced.

Unblinded care team. Mortality is objective; potential bias in withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy was mitigated by structured neuroprognostication. Withdrawal within 10 days was similar (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.88–1.40, P=0.38; median 5 days IQR 3–8 in both).

Screened 1431, randomised 950. Consent withdrawn in 1/476 (0.2%) in 33°C vs 3/474 (0.6%) in 36°C. Final modified ITT n=473 vs n=466. Per-protocol n=472 vs n=464. 180-day CPC/mRS complete for 469/473 and 464/466.

Crossovers rare (received wrong target 0 vs 1). Clear temperature separation achieved on Day 2 (36.0±1.5°C vs 37.2±0.7°C, P<0.001); fever prevented in both arms (hours >38°C median 0 vs 0, P=0.070; rebound >39°C 0 vs 0).

Groups matched for witnessed arrest (93% vs 93%), bystander CPR (74% vs 75%), initial shockable rhythm (359/473 [76%] vs 348/466 [75%]), day 1 angiography (60% vs 61%), day 1 PCI (40% vs 39%), shock at admission (15% vs 14%), and STEMI (40% vs 42%). Median ICU LOS 8 vs 8 days; hospital LOS 11 vs 10 days.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong given concealed randomisation, complete follow-up, and clear temperature separation, with main potential risk being unblinded care delivery.

domains.notes: Enrolled mostly witnessed OHCA with high rates of bystander CPR and shockable rhythms. Excluded unwitnessed asystolic arrests, non-cardiac causes, severe initial hypothermia (<30°C), or delayed screening (>240 min post-ROSC).
Highly generalisable to adult comatose OHCA survivors managed in well-resourced ICUs with protocolised temperature management and structured post-arrest care pathways.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for comatose adult OHCA survivors in modern ICU settings, but limited for non-cardiac arrests, unwitnessed asystole, or resource-constrained environments.

strengths: Large, international multicentre design across 36 ICUs with robust power.
Near-complete follow-up at 180 days for primary and secondary outcomes.
Active temperature control and fever prevention used in both arms, directly isolating target temperature.
Structured protocol for neuroprognostication and withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy to limit bias.
limitations: Open-label design may influence clinical decision-making or co-interventions.
Enrolled up to 4 hours post-ROSC, leaving ultra-early or intra-arrest cooling unstudied.
CPC and mRS functional scales are relatively coarse outcome measures.
Increased rate of hypokalaemia and occasional early rewarming due to instability in the 33°C group.

critical_appraisal.summary: Landmark trial demonstrating that hypothermia at 33°C is not superior to 36°C when fever is actively controlled in both groups.
strengths: Enforced active temperature control in control group
weaknesses: Window up to 4 hours post-ROSC before initiation

sections.authors_conclusion: In comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause, targeted temperature management at 33°C did not confer a survival or functional benefit compared to 36°C.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: 33°C targeted hypothermia does not improve survival or neurological recovery over 36°C controlled normothermia with fever prevention.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Comatose adult survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Temperature control is unnecessary; uncontrolled fever must still be actively prevented.
implementation_caveats: Active temperature management and fever prevention must be strictly maintained if targeting 36°C.
If 33°C is used, monitor closely for hypokalaemia, shivering, and hemodynamic instability.

controversies.topic: Misinterpretation as absence of temperature control
controversies.notes: TTM compared two active temperature management protocols (33°C vs 36°C with fever prevention in both), not hypothermia versus passive care.
Inclusion allowed up to 240 minutes post-ROSC, raising questions whether immediate intra-arrest cooling might yield different results.
Subsequent trials (TTM2) confirmed these findings, solidifying targeted normothermia and fever prevention as standard of care.

context_related_trials.relation: Follow-up RCT in 2021 comparing 33°C hypothermia to targeted normothermia (fever prevention), confirming no survival benefit and higher arrhythmia rates with hypothermia.

unresolved_questions: Does intra-arrest or ultra-early cooling initiated immediately at ROSC provide neuroprotection?
Are there specific patient subgroups or biological endotypes that derive benefit from 33°C cooling?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Target 36°C with active fever control instead of 33°C hypothermia post-OHCA to avoid cooling side effects without sacrificing survival or neurological recovery.
